Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he's willing to hold elections if President Trump can get Russia to suspend its attacks on Ukraine for 60 days.
Terry Schultz reports Zelensky also weighed in on Trump's deal to import Russian diesel fuel.
Addressing the annual Warsaw Security Forum conference, President Zelensky said while holding elections during a war would require changing Ukrainian law,
it would be possible if Russian attacks ceased so that people could safely take part in the process. He's heard here through an interpreter.
And it's also impossible now because of our military, more than a million people who must vote, but how will they vote while being on the front line?
Zelensky also suggested that instead of buying diesel from Russia, the U.S. should buy from Ukraine.
He said he'd been given no advance notification of the agreement with the Kremlin that Trump announced Friday.
For NPR News, I'm Terry Schultz in Warsaw.
As promoting President Trump and his policies continued being paid for by the U.S. government, well, after Trump said his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over.
NPR's Tamara Keith reports the administration is now under a court order to take them down.
When President Trump announced the U.S. government would no longer be paying for the "patriotic ads," about $12 million had already been spent.
But despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the ads didn't stop airing.
In the intervening week, another $10 million in taxpayer dollars went to fund the pro-Trump ads.
That's according to an NPR analysis of ad impact data.
On Sunday, a federal judge issued a temporary order barring future airings.
A White House official, not authorized to speak publicly, says the last ads paid for by the government aired on Sunday evening.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Israel's Supreme Court is ordering officials to plan for the return of Palestinians to their homes in the occupied West Bank.
NPR's Daniel Estrin says tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced from their communities for more than a year.
The Israeli Supreme Court has ordered the Israeli military to specify a timeline for when Palestinian civilians can return to their homes in several West Bank refugee camps.
Israel evacuated and largely destroyed those areas during a military operation more than a year and a half ago.
Israel said it was countering militant strongholds.
It's the largest mass displacement in the West Bank in many decades.
Infrastructure still hasn't been rebuilt, and families haven't been allowed to return.
An Israeli cabinet minister is calling to ignore the court ruling.
Faisal Salama, the Palestinian leader of one displaced refugee camp, called the court ruling "useless,"
as long as the Israeli military continues to occupy the area.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
U.S. futures contracts are trading in mixed territory at this hour.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The United States is in the midst of the biggest and deadliest measles epidemics in decades.
With cases reported across the country, infectious disease experts say some vaccinated adults should consider getting another measles shot.
And Piers Maria Godoy has more.
Before vaccines, measles used to kill four to five hundred people in the U.S. each year.
Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is 97 percent effective.
Most people vaccinated before 1989 probably received just one dose instead of the two doses recommended for children today.
Dr. Larry Kousiolek of Northwestern University says traditionally,
one dose has been considered sufficient protection for adults not at high risk.
But he says these days...
If you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose.
If you're not sure of your vaccination history, he says there's no harm in getting an extra dose of the MMR vaccine.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
A consumer lawsuit in Illinois is challenging McDonald's over software that restaurants can use to help set prices.
The suit claims the software allows competing franchisees to share information they ordinarily would not.
Pumpkin Competition is serious business and there appears to be a record setting squash in Rhode Island.
Ron Wallace's giant pumpkin weighed in at 3,156 pounds at a contest in New England.
That's the weight of nearly three grand pianos. And he won $3,500 for it.
